title: Transfer Learning in High-dimensional Ising Models
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: Our transfer method steadily reduces error as informative sources are added, beating target-only and naive pooling across graph structures and perturbation levels.
layout: 2x2 grid of graph types, each with three line-plot panels
description: A 2x2 grid of blocks, each titled with a graph structure: Random Sparse, Block-wise Star, Chain, and Sparse Block Star. Each block holds three small line plots for perturbation = 1, 10 and 20. The x-axis is the number of auxiliary sources |A|, running 0 to 12. The y-axis is average relative error. A flat red line (Naive-LogLasso) stays near 0.85. A cyan line with squares (Pooled-Trans-Ising) starts high, at about 1.2 to 2.2, and falls steeply. A green triangle line (Oracle-Trans-Ising) and a purple dashed line (Trans-Ising) overlap, drop quickly to about 0.3, and stay lowest. The curves look nearly the same across panels, though the cyan line moves a little with perturbation. A shared legend sits at the bottom. The eye goes first to the bold graph titles, then to the falling curves.
caption: Average relative errors for Naive-LogLasso (red), Oracle Trans-Ising (green), Pooled-Trans-Ising (cyan), and Trans-Ising (purple), across four graph structures at perturbation levels $100\sigma\in\{1,10,20\}$, with $p=200$.
abstract: In high-dimensional Ising model estimation, target sample sizes are often limited, and effectively using auxiliary binary datasets of unknown relevance remains challenging. To address this, we propose Trans-Ising, a transfer learning method that combines a loss-based source screening rule with a two-stage estimation procedure. The method first identifies informative auxiliary sources using held-out target pseudolikelihood to prevent negative transfer. It then computes an initial estimator via pooled nodewise $\ell_1$-regularized logistic regression, followed by a target-only correction step using a folded-concave penalty. Theoretically, we establish fixed-node $\ell_2$ and $\ell_1$ error bounds, exact graph selection consistency, and the conditional consistency of the screening rule. Through extensive simulations and real-data analyses, we demonstrate that Trans-Ising achieves lower estimation errors than both target-only estimation and naive data pooling.
